brief.summary: Analysis software for academic machine-learning interpretability labs that study the internal features of language models learned by sparse autoencoders, letting researchers relate feature statistics, labels and examples across layers.
brief.user: Kofi Mensah, a third-year PhD student in a university interpretability lab who trained sparse autoencoders on an open 1-billion-parameter language model and is writing a workshop paper due in three weeks.
brief.moment: His advisor questioned a claim in his draft: that features with very high activation frequency are mostly uninterpretable 'dense' junk. Kofi has to find out whether that holds across layers or only in later ones, whether automated interpretability scores are lower for dense features or just less reliable, and whether a cluster of features in layer 12 that all fire on code tokens breaks the pattern. He needs to slice the features by layer, compare frequency against interpretability score, pick out exceptions, and read top-activating text examples for a handful of them before tomorrow's lab meeting.
brief.data: 8 sparse autoencoders, one per sampled layer (layers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16), each with 16,384 features: 131,072 in total. Per feature: layer, index, activation frequency (from 1e-7 to 0.4), mean and max activation, dead or alive (about 9% dead), an auto-generated label (e.g. 'Python function definitions', 'French negation'), an automated interpretability score from 0 to 1 with a confidence interval, a human label on 600 hand-reviewed features, and the top 20 activating text snippets with token-level activations. Cosine similarity of decoder vectors for nearest neighbors across adjacent layers. Training metadata: 2B tokens, L0 sparsity per layer 18–64, reconstruction loss. Kofi's working notes with 3 hypotheses and 41 bookmarked features.

prompt:
I need the front end for Featurescope. Analysis software for academic machine-learning interpretability labs that study the internal features of language models learned by sparse autoencoders, letting researchers relate feature statistics, labels and examples across layers.

Who's using it: Kofi Mensah, a third-year PhD student in a university interpretability lab who trained sparse autoencoders on an open 1-billion-parameter language model and is writing a workshop paper due in three weeks.

What they're doing right now: His advisor questioned a claim in his draft: that features with very high activation frequency are mostly uninterpretable 'dense' junk. Kofi has to find out whether that holds across layers or only in later ones, whether automated interpretability scores are lower for dense features or just less reliable, and whether a cluster of features in layer 12 that all fire on code tokens breaks the pattern. He needs to slice the features by layer, compare frequency against interpretability score, pick out exceptions, and read top-activating text examples for a handful of them before tomorrow's lab meeting.

What's in the system at this point: 8 sparse autoencoders, one per sampled layer (layers 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16), each with 16,384 features: 131,072 in total. Per feature: layer, index, activation frequency (from 1e-7 to 0.4), mean and max activation, dead or alive (about 9% dead), an auto-generated label (e.g. 'Python function definitions', 'French negation'), an automated interpretability score from 0 to 1 with a confidence interval, a human label on 600 hand-reviewed features, and the top 20 activating text snippets with token-level activations. Cosine similarity of decoder vectors for nearest neighbors across adjacent layers. Training metadata: 2B tokens, L0 sparsity per layer 18–64, reconstruction loss. Kofi's working notes with 3 hypotheses and 41 bookmarked features.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
